marrow__BIOCHEM_CH20_Q001.takeaway: Basal metabolic rate tracks metabolically active lean body mass more closely than total size measures.
marrow__BIOCHEM_CH20_Q001.displayText:
Basal metabolic rate tracks metabolically active lean body mass more closely than total size measures.

Basal metabolic rate (BMR) is closely dependent on lean body mass (fat-free mass).
Lean body mass is the difference between total body weight and body fat weight. It is the metabolically active tissue in the body.
The BMR decreases with increasing age, even when body weight remains constant. This is the result of muscle tissue replacement by adipose tissue, which is metabolically less active. Women have a significantly lower BMR than men of the same body weight and age. This is because women’s bodies contain proportionally more adipose tissue.
emphasis: Basal metabolic rate tracks metabolically active lean body mass more closely than total size measures

rationales.a: Body surface area can be used to estimate energy expenditure, but lean mass is the key physiological determinant asked here.
rationales.c: BMI combines weight and height but cannot distinguish metabolically active muscle from adipose tissue.
rationales.d: A height-to-weight ratio does not measure the amount of metabolically active tissue that drives basal energy needs.

sourceNotes: Source question/key: ED8 Biochemistry p. 318; explanation p. 323.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH20_Q002.takeaway: Starvation lowers basal metabolic rate as the body adapts to prolonged energy restriction.
marrow__BIOCHEM_CH20_Q002.displayText:
Starvation lowers basal metabolic rate as the body adapts to prolonged energy restriction.

Decreased basal metabolic rate (BMR) is seen in starvation.
emphasis: Starvation lowers basal metabolic rate as the body adapts to prolonged energy restriction

rationales.b: Cachexia is a catabolic illness state and does not represent the classic adaptive fall in BMR from food deprivation tested here.
rationales.c: Cold exposure generally increases thermogenesis and energy expenditure rather than lowering BMR.
rationales.d: Excess thyroid hormone raises metabolic rate; it does not cause a low BMR.

sourceNotes: Source question/key: ED8 Biochemistry p. 318; explanation p. 323.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH20_Q003.takeaway: Intestinal bacteria can synthesize biotin, vitamin K and pantothenate; niacin is formed from tryptophan in human metabolism.
marrow__BIOCHEM_CH20_Q003.displayText:
Intestinal bacteria can synthesize biotin, vitamin K and pantothenate; niacin is formed from tryptophan in human metabolism.

Niacin is not synthesized by the bacterial flora in the intestine.
Endogenously synthesized vitamins can be derived from 2 sources:
Synthesized by the body
Synthesized in the body (by bacterial flora in the intestine)
Niacin: synthesized from an amino acid tryptophan
Vitamin D: synthesized from 7 Dehydrocholesterol by exposure to UV-B rays (290-315 nm) in the skin.
Vitamin K
Biotin
Pantothenic Acid
emphasis: Intestinal bacteria can synthesize biotin, vitamin K and pantothenate; niacin is formed from tryptophan in human metabolism

rationales.b: Biotin is synthesized by intestinal bacterial flora and is among the listed microbial vitamin products.
rationales.c: Vitamin K₂ (menaquinone) is synthesized by gut bacteria, so it is not the exception.
rationales.d: Pantothenic acid can be produced by intestinal flora; niacin's endogenous synthesis instead uses tryptophan.

sourceNotes: Source question/key: ED8 Biochemistry p. 318; explanation p. 323.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH20_Q004.takeaway: RDA is set about two standard deviations above the EAR to cover the needs of nearly all healthy people in a group.
marrow__BIOCHEM_CH20_Q004.displayText:
RDA is set about two standard deviations above the EAR to cover the needs of nearly all healthy people in a group.

Recommended dietary allowance (RDA) is calculated by using the formula, RDA = EAR + 2SD.
Estimated average requirement (EAR): The EAR is the average daily nutrient intake level estimated to meet the requirement of one-half of healthy individuals in a particular life stage and gender group.
Recommended dietary allowance (RDA): The RDA is the average daily dietary intake level that is sufficient to meet the nutrient requirements of nearly all individuals in a life stage and gender group. The RDA is calculated based on EAR and is set above the EAR to provide a margin of safety for most individuals. So, RDA is set 2SDs above the EAR.
emphasis: RDA is set about two standard deviations above the EAR to cover the needs of nearly all healthy people in a group

rationales.b: Two standard deviations below EAR would fall below the estimated need for half of the group, not protect nearly all individuals.
rationales.c: EAR meets the estimated requirement of only about half of the group; RDA is set higher.
rationales.d: RDA is derived by adding two standard deviations to EAR, not by simply doubling it.

sourceNotes: Source question/key: ED8 Biochemistry p. 318; explanation p. 324.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH20_Q005.takeaway: The source table assigns 400 μg/day as the vitamin A RDA for a six-year-old child.
marrow__BIOCHEM_CH20_Q005.displayText:
The source table assigns 400 μg/day as the vitamin A RDA for a six-year-old child.

Recommended dietary allowance (RDA) of vitamin A in a 6-year-old child is 400mcg/day.
Sources of vitamin A:
Animal source: liver, egg, butter, milk, fish, meat
Richest plant source: carrot
Richest source: halibut liver oil (fish oil)
emphasis: The source table assigns 400 μg/day as the vitamin A RDA for a six-year-old child

rationales.a: 700 μg/day is above the age-specific value given by the source table for a six-year-old.
rationales.b: 800 μg/day is not the source table's RDA for this age; it exceeds the listed 400 μg/day.
rationales.d: 300 μg/day is below the age-specific source-table recommendation of 400 μg/day.

sourceNotes: Source question/key: ED8 Biochemistry p. 319; explanation p. 324.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH20_Q007.takeaway: Excess vitamin A can cause intracranial hypertension with headache, papilledema and visual symptoms (pseudotumor cerebri).
marrow__BIOCHEM_CH20_Q007.displayText:
Excess vitamin A can cause intracranial hypertension with headache, papilledema and visual symptoms (pseudotumor cerebri).

The clinical scenario of increased intracranial pressure in the absence of space-occupying lesion points towards the diagnosis of pseudotumor cerebri. Vitamin A excess is the likely cause.
Clinical features of hypervitaminosis A:
CNS: Symptoms of raised intracranial pressure (pseudotumor cerebri) such as headache, nausea, vomiting, blurring of vision, ataxia, anorexia
Liver: Hepatomegaly and hyperlipidemia
Musculoskeletal: Thickening of the long bones (bony exostosis), hypercalcemia, soft tissue calcification
Dermatological: Dryness, exfoliative dermatitis, alopecia
Teratogenesis: Pregnant women should not ingest excessive quantities as it can cause congenital malformations in the developing fetus. Isotretinoin(13-cis retinoic acid) is a drug that is teratogenic and absolutely contraindicated in pregnancy.
emphasis: Excess vitamin A can cause intracranial hypertension with headache, papilledema and visual symptoms (pseudotumor cerebri)

rationales.b: Vitamin D excess is associated with hypercalcemia and soft-tissue calcification, not the characteristic retinoid-associated pseudotumor picture.
rationales.c: Vitamin E toxicity is not the classic cause of raised intracranial pressure in this setting.
rationales.d: Vitamin K excess is not the vitamin toxicity associated with papilledema and pseudotumor cerebri.

sourceNotes: Source question/key: ED8 Biochemistry p. 319; explanation p. 325.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH20_Q008.takeaway: Polar bear liver is exceptionally rich in stored retinol; eating it can cause acute hypervitaminosis A.
marrow__BIOCHEM_CH20_Q008.displayText:
Polar bear liver is exceptionally rich in stored retinol; eating it can cause acute hypervitaminosis A.

The clinical scenario is suggestive of vitamin A toxicity. Polar bear livers should not be consumed as they can cause vitamin A toxicity and death.
Vitamin A and other fat soluble vitamins are stored particularly in the liver and adipose tissue.
Vitamins can be broadly classified into two categories:
Fat-soluble vitamins: Vitamins A, D, E, K
Water-soluble vitamins: Vitamin B complex and vitamin C
Properties of fat-soluble vitamins:
Hydrophobic in nature
Transported in blood by the lipoproteins, such as chylomicrons
Stored in the liver and the adipose tissue
emphasis: Polar bear liver is exceptionally rich in stored retinol; eating it can cause acute hypervitaminosis A

rationales.a: Kidneys are not the organ identified in the source for the dangerous retinol load; polar bear liver stores very high vitamin A.
rationales.b: The spleen is not the reservoir implicated in this toxicity; the liver contains concentrated vitamin A stores.
rationales.c: Muscle is not the source's high-risk organ for this acute retinol exposure; polar bear liver is.

sourceNotes: Source question/key: ED8 Biochemistry p. 319; explanation p. 325.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH20_Q009.takeaway: Chronic vitamin A excess causes raised, not reduced, intracranial pressure; it can also cause ataxia, hepatomegaly and alopecia.
marrow__BIOCHEM_CH20_Q009.displayText:
Chronic vitamin A excess causes raised, not reduced, intracranial pressure; it can also cause ataxia, hepatomegaly and alopecia.

The clinical scenario is suggestive of vitamin A toxicity. It causes increased intracranial pressure, not reduced intracranial pressure.
In cases of chronic ingestion, the accumulation of vitamin A goes beyond the capacity of intracellular binding proteins producing hypervitaminosis.
Clinical features of hypervitaminosis A:
CNS: Symptoms of raised intracranial pressure (pseudotumor cerebri) such as headache, nausea, vomiting, blurring of vision, ataxia, anorexia
Liver: Hepatomegaly and hyperlipidemia
Musculoskeletal: Thickening of the long bones (bony exostosis), hypercalcemia, soft tissue calcification
Dermatological: Dryness, exfoliative dermatitis, alopecia
Teratogenesis: Pregnant women should not ingest excessive quantities as it can cause congenital malformations in the developing fetus. Isotretinoin (13-cis retinoic acid) is a vitamin A derived drug that is teratogenic and absolutely contraindicated in pregnancy.
emphasis: Chronic vitamin A excess causes raised, not reduced, intracranial pressure; it can also cause ataxia, hepatomegaly and alopecia

rationales.a: Ataxia is among the neurologic manifestations of chronic vitamin A toxicity, so it is associated.
rationales.c: Vitamin A accumulation can cause hepatomegaly and hyperlipidemia, making this a toxicity feature.
rationales.d: Alopecia and other skin changes occur in hypervitaminosis A, so it is associated.

sourceNotes: Source question/key: ED8 Biochemistry p. 320; explanation p. 326.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH20_Q010.takeaway: Vitamin D metabolites act as steroid hormones, regulating calcium/phosphate balance and other cellular functions.
marrow__BIOCHEM_CH20_Q010.displayText:
Vitamin D metabolites act as steroid hormones, regulating calcium/phosphate balance and other cellular functions.

Vitamin D is also considered a hormone.
Vitamin D encompasses a group of sterols, which have a hormone-like function.
Functions of vitamin D:
Regulation of calcium and phosphate: It increased blood calcium and phosphate level
Immunomodulatory action: Vitamin D increases the ability of the innate immune system to fight against pathogens
Antiproliferative: Because of the antiproliferative function, deficiency (<20ng/ml) is associated with an increased incidence of colon cancer, breast cancer, prostate cancer
Bone development
emphasis: Vitamin D metabolites act as steroid hormones, regulating calcium/phosphate balance and other cellular functions

rationales.a: Vitamin E is primarily a lipid-phase antioxidant; it is not the vitamin with hormone-like endocrine activity asked here.
rationales.b: Vitamin C is a water-soluble reducing agent and enzyme cofactor, not the steroid-like hormone in this group.
rationales.d: Vitamin K supports γ-carboxylation of clotting proteins; it is not considered a hormone.

sourceNotes: Source question/key: ED8 Biochemistry p. 320; explanation p. 326.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH20_Q011.takeaway: The liver performs the first hydroxylation of cholecalciferol to 25-hydroxyvitamin D; the kidney forms active 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D.
marrow__BIOCHEM_CH20_Q011.displayText:
The liver performs the first hydroxylation of cholecalciferol to 25-hydroxyvitamin D; the kidney forms active 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D.

The first hydroxylation of vitamin D takes place in the liver to form 25-hydroxycholecalciferol.
Vitamin D, as either cholecalciferol or ergocalciferol does not have significant biological activity. It is activated in the following steps:
Skin: 7-Dehydrocholesterol (an intermediate in the synthesis of cholesterol in the skin) undergoes a nonenzymic reaction on exposure to ultraviolet light (290nm to 315nm), yielding cholecalciferol.
Liver: Cholecalciferol is hydroxylated to 25-hydroxycholecalciferol (the most abundant circulatory form of Vitamin D) by the enzyme 25-hydroxylase.
Kidney: 25-hydroxycholecalciferol is converted to 1,25 dihydroxycholecalciferol (calcitriol), the biologically active form by the enzyme 1α-hydroxylase.
Calcitriol acts on the bone, intestine, and kidney to maintain calcium and phosphate homeostasis. If the body does not require vitamin D, in the kidney, 24-hydroxylase converts vitamin D into 24,25 dihydroxycholecalciferol, which is an inactive metabolite.
emphasis: The liver performs the first hydroxylation of cholecalciferol to 25-hydroxyvitamin D; the kidney forms active 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D

rationales.a: Skin initiates vitamin D production by UVB conversion of 7-dehydrocholesterol, but this is photochemical synthesis, not the first hydroxylation.
rationales.b: The kidney performs the later 1α-hydroxylation that produces calcitriol, not the initial 25-hydroxylation.
rationales.d: The small intestine is a target for vitamin D action, not the organ that carries out its first hydroxylation.

sourceNotes: Source question/key: ED8 Biochemistry p. 320; explanation p. 327.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH20_Q012.takeaway: Vitamin D regulates mineral balance and can modulate immunity and proliferation; antioxidant activity is not its defining function.
marrow__BIOCHEM_CH20_Q012.displayText:
Vitamin D regulates mineral balance and can modulate immunity and proliferation; antioxidant activity is not its defining function.

Vitamin D is not an antioxidant.
Functions of vitamin D:
Regulation of calcium and phosphate: It increases blood calcium and phosphate level
Immunomodulatory action: Vitamin D increases the ability of the innate immune system to fight against pathogens
Antiproliferative: Because of the antiproliferative function, deficiency(<20ng/ml) is associated with an increased incidence of colon cancer, breast cancer, prostate cancer
Bone development
emphasis: Vitamin D regulates mineral balance and can modulate immunity and proliferation; antioxidant activity is not its defining function

rationales.a: Vitamin D has immunomodulatory effects through regulation of immune-cell signaling.
rationales.b: Vitamin D promotes intestinal absorption and homeostatic regulation of phosphate, along with calcium.
rationales.d: Vitamin D signaling has antiproliferative effects in several tissues, unlike a direct antioxidant role.

sourceNotes: Source question/key: ED8 Biochemistry p. 321; explanation p. 327.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH20_Q013.takeaway: Vitamin E is the principal lipid-soluble, chain-breaking antioxidant that protects membranes from peroxidation.
marrow__BIOCHEM_CH20_Q013.displayText:
Vitamin E is the principal lipid-soluble, chain-breaking antioxidant that protects membranes from peroxidation.

Vitamin E is the most potent and naturally occurring antioxidant.
Current therapeutic use of vitamin E is recommended in diseases that cause fat malabsorption, severe pancreatic insufficiency, and cholestatic liver disease.
Protective antioxidant nutrients:
Vitamin E
Vitamin C
Vitamin A and the carotenoids
Selenium
Polyphenolic compounds derived from plant foods
emphasis: Vitamin E is the principal lipid-soluble, chain-breaking antioxidant that protects membranes from peroxidation

rationales.a: β-carotene is an antioxidant nutrient, but the source identifies vitamin E as the most potent naturally occurring antioxidant among these choices.
rationales.c: Vitamin C is a water-soluble antioxidant that can regenerate oxidized vitamin E, but is not the principal lipid-phase antioxidant here.
rationales.d: Vitamin A and its carotenoid precursors have antioxidant roles, but the source's strongest natural antioxidant answer is vitamin E.

sourceNotes: Source question/key: ED8 Biochemistry p. 321; explanation p. 328.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH20_Q014.takeaway: Vitamin E deficiency can destabilize erythrocyte membranes and cause hemolytic anemia because antioxidant protection is lost.
marrow__BIOCHEM_CH20_Q014.displayText:
Vitamin E deficiency can destabilize erythrocyte membranes and cause hemolytic anemia because antioxidant protection is lost.

The clinical scenario of a patient with fatigue and decreased hemoglobin, increased indirect bilirubin, and increased LDH is suggestive of hemolytic anemia. It is associated with a deficiency of vitamin E.
The most important function of vitamin E is its chain-breaking antioxidant role. Vitamin E inhibits lipid peroxidation by free radicals, thereby stabilizing cell membranes. Hence, its deficiency can result in erythrocyte membranes being abnormally fragile leading to hemolytic anemia.
Note: Vitamin K deficiency does not cause hemolysis. It causes manifestations of impaired coagulation, such as easy bruisability, mucosal bleeding, etc. However, vitamin K toxicity can cause hemolysis.
emphasis: Vitamin E deficiency can destabilize erythrocyte membranes and cause hemolytic anemia because antioxidant protection is lost

rationales.a: Vitamin A deficiency causes visual and epithelial abnormalities rather than the membrane-fragility hemolysis described.
rationales.c: Vitamin D deficiency chiefly disrupts bone/mineral homeostasis; it does not explain antioxidant-related RBC fragility.
rationales.d: Vitamin K deficiency impairs coagulation and causes bleeding; it is not the deficiency classically associated with hemolytic anemia.

sourceNotes: Source question/key: ED8 Biochemistry p. 321; explanation p. 328.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH20_Q015.takeaway: Vitamin K supports γ-carboxylation of clotting proteins and is the fat-soluble vitamin with coenzyme activity.
marrow__BIOCHEM_CH20_Q015.displayText:
Vitamin K supports γ-carboxylation of clotting proteins and is the fat-soluble vitamin with coenzyme activity.

The only fat-soluble vitamin that has a coenzyme function is vitamin K.
The co-enzyme role of vitamin K is in the γ-carboxylation reaction of clotting factors.
Many of the water-soluble vitamins also have a coenzyme function, such as:
Vitamin B1 as thiamine pyrophosphate (TPP)
Vitamin B6 as pyridoxal phosphate (PLP)
emphasis: Vitamin K supports γ-carboxylation of clotting proteins and is the fat-soluble vitamin with coenzyme activity

rationales.a: Vitamin A functions in vision and gene regulation but is not the fat-soluble vitamin coenzyme in carboxylation.
rationales.b: Vitamin D is a hormone-like regulator of mineral balance, not a coenzyme in clotting-factor modification.
rationales.c: Vitamin E is a chain-breaking antioxidant; it does not serve as the carboxylation coenzyme.

sourceNotes: Source question/key: ED8 Biochemistry p. 321; explanation p. 329.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH20_Q016.takeaway: Long antibiotic courses can deplete intestinal flora-derived menaquinone and contribute to vitamin K deficiency.
marrow__BIOCHEM_CH20_Q016.displayText:
Long antibiotic courses can deplete intestinal flora-derived menaquinone and contribute to vitamin K deficiency.

Prolonged use of antibiotics leads to vitamin K deficiency. This is due to the loss of normal bowel flora that synthesizes menaquinones (vitamin K2).
Vitamin K is a fat-soluble vitamin. The following are the vitamers of vitamin K:
Phylloquinone (Vitamin K1) is the normal dietary source of Vitamin K that is found in green vegetables.
Menaquinones (Vitamin K2) are synthesized by intestinal bacteria.
Menadione (Vitamin K3) is a synthetic compound that is metabolized to phylloquinone.
emphasis: Long antibiotic courses can deplete intestinal flora-derived menaquinone and contribute to vitamin K deficiency

rationales.a: Vitamin K deficiency causes impaired γ-carboxylation and bleeding tendency, not hypercoagulability.
rationales.b: Vitamin K is fat soluble, so this statement misclassifies its absorption/storage category.
rationales.d: Green vegetables are the dietary source of phylloquinone (K₁); menaquinone (K₂) is produced by bacteria.

sourceNotes: Source question/key: ED8 Biochemistry p. 322; explanation p. 329.

marrow__BIOCHEM_CH20_Q017.takeaway: Warfarin impairs vitamin K-dependent γ-carboxylation of II, VII, IX and X; factor VIII is not vitamin K dependent.
marrow__BIOCHEM_CH20_Q017.displayText:
Warfarin impairs vitamin K-dependent γ-carboxylation of II, VII, IX and X; factor VIII is not vitamin K dependent.

Warfarin, which is an oral anticoagulant drug inhibits gamma-carboxylation of clotting factors II, VII, IX, and X, but not factor VIII. Thus, the levels of clotting factor VIII will be unaffected in her.
Warfarin inhibits vitamin K epoxide reductase, an enzyme required for the reduction of vitamin K. Reduced vitamin K is involved in the post-translational modification of blood clotting factors such as prothrombin (factor II), factor VII, factor IX, factor X, protein C, and protein S.
Therefore, warfarin indirectly inhibits the gamma-carboxylation reaction or post-translational modification of blood clotting factors.
emphasis: Warfarin impairs vitamin K-dependent γ-carboxylation of II, VII, IX and X; factor VIII is not vitamin K dependent

rationales.a: Factor II requires vitamin K-dependent γ-carboxylation, so warfarin affects its functional maturation.
rationales.b: Factor VII is vitamin K dependent and is affected by warfarin-mediated blockade of vitamin K recycling.
rationales.d: Factor X is vitamin K dependent and its γ-carboxylation is inhibited during warfarin therapy.

sourceNotes: Source question/key: ED8 Biochemistry p. 322; explanation p. 329,330.
